scenario.context: A startup wants to launch premium pet-food delivery in Bengaluru.

steps.task: Estimate the annual market size in rupees, stating every assumption.
hints: Funnel down to buyers of premium food.

content.sanity: ₹1,500 a month is plausible for one medium dog on premium food; compare against any known metro pet-food estimate and discuss serviceable share (maybe 10 to 20% via delivery).

reference.whyItWorks: Clear funnel with round numbers that are easy to challenge and replace.
commonMistakes: Starting with a huge top-down figure and no logic

scenario.context: A quick-commerce app has 800,000 monthly ordering users and an AOV of ₹500. Product wants to add pay-later at checkout and needs the incremental GMV opportunity.

steps.task: Estimate the annual incremental GMV from the feature and list the 3 assumptions that matter most.
hints: Think adoption, frequency, and basket uplift.
Be careful to count only incremental value.

content.formula: Incremental GMV = orders placed by adopters × incremental basket per order = 320,000 × ₹75
content.result: ≈ ₹2.4 crore a month ≈ ₹29 crore a year
content.sanity: Key assumptions: 10% adoption, 15% uplift, no cannibalisation. Also note possible extra revenue from fees and risk cost from defaults.

reference.whyItWorks: Isolates the increment rather than counting total GMV from adopters.
commonMistakes: Counting all adopter GMV as new

title: AI meeting notes for Indian SMEs

scenario.context: A startup is building an AI meeting-notes tool for small and medium businesses in India and needs a market estimate for the board.

steps.task: Estimate the annual revenue opportunity using both a top-down and a bottom-up approach and reconcile the two.
hints: Top-down: pick a known broader market and take a share.

content.formula: Bottom-up: 28,800 accounts × 6 seats × ₹600 × 12 = ₹43,200 per account a year. Top-down: take the Indian SME software-spend pool and assume meeting tools capture a small share.
content.result: Bottom-up ≈ ₹124 crore a year; top-down should land in the same order of magnitude (₹100 to 200 crore)
content.sanity: Reconcile: if the two differ by more than 2 to 3 times, revisit adoption and price. Biggest unknowns: adoption rate and price sensitivity.

reference.whyItWorks: Two methods cross-check each other and expose the weakest assumptions.
commonMistakes: Treating total addressable market as expected revenue
